title: 2 Samuel 21:15–22
context: Brief reports of later Philistine wars: an aging David nearly falls, and his men kill four warriors described as born to the giant in Gath. WEB’s wording at 21:19 bears on 1 Samuel 17 and 1 Chronicles 20:5.

verses.text: The Philistines had war again with Israel; and David went down, and his servants with him, and fought against the Philistines. David grew faint;
verses.arminianNotes: In renewed war with the Philistines, “David grew faint.” Arminian readers see a once-mighty warrior now showing his age and limits, which the narrative presents honestly.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see David’s weakness exposed. The appendix to 2 Samuel shows that even God’s anointed king depends on others and ultimately on the LORD for victory.

verses.text: and Ishbibenob, who was of the sons of the giant, the weight of whose spear was three hundred shekels of bronze in weight, he being armed with a new sword, thought he would kill David.
verses.arminianNotes: Ishbibenob, “of the sons of the giant,” with a heavy bronze spear and a new sword, thinks he will kill David. Arminian readers see David in real danger, with no guarantee apart from faithful companions.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the threat to the king’s life. The detail of the spear’s weight underlines the danger and sets up the rescue that follows in the next verse.

verses.text: But Abishai the son of Zeruiah helped him, and struck the Philistine and killed him. Then the men of David swore to him, saying, “Don’t go out with us to battle any more, so that you don’t quench the lamp of Israel.”
verses.arminianNotes: Abishai rescues David, and his men swear, “Don’t go out with us to battle any more, so that you don’t quench the lamp of Israel.” Arminian readers see the king’s life valued as vital to the nation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the “lamp of Israel” image expressing hope bound up with David’s line. Many readers in this tradition connect it with God’s promise to preserve David’s house.

verses.text: After this, there was again war with the Philistines at Gob. Then Sibbecai the Hushathite killed Saph, who was of the sons of the giant.
verses.arminianNotes: At Gob, Sibbecai the Hushathite kills Saph, “of the sons of the giant.” Arminian readers see faithful servants sharing in the victories once associated mainly with David himself.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God giving victory through David’s men. The list honors those who fought alongside the king, and readers in this tradition note that deliverance is not tied to one hero.

verses.text: There was again war with the Philistines at Gob, and Elhanan the son of Jaare-Oregim the Bethlehemite killed Goliath the Gittite’s brother, the staff of whose spear was like a weaver’s beam.
verses.arminianNotes: WEB prints that Elhanan “killed Goliath the Gittite’s brother,” and this edition has no footnote here. Arminian readers note that 1 Chronicles 20:5 names the brother Lahmi, and that the relation of this verse to 1 Samuel 17 is a well-known difficulty already mentioned there; translations of 2 Samuel 21:19 differ.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise acknowledge the difficulty. The proposals commonly noted at 1 Samuel 17 are held as proposals, not settled conclusions, and these notes declare no winner.

verses.text: There was again war at Gath, where there was a man of great stature, who had six fingers on every hand and six toes on every foot, twenty-four in number, and he also was born to the giant.
verses.arminianNotes: At Gath a man of great stature with six fingers and six toes, “born to the giant,” appears. Arminian readers see the narrator recording a remarkable opponent to show the scale of the threat Israel faced.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the description emphasizing Israel’s formidable enemies. The verse continues the list without elaboration, and readers in this tradition generally do not speculate beyond the details given.

verses.text: When he defied Israel, Jonathan the son of Shimei, David’s brother, killed him.
verses.arminianNotes: When he defies Israel, “Jonathan the son of Shimei, David’s brother,” kills him. Arminian readers see an echo of David’s own victory over a defiant giant in 1 Samuel 17.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note that the language of defying Israel recalls Goliath. God continues to deliver his people through faithful servants from David’s own family.

verses.text: These four were born to the giant in Gath; and they fell by the hand of David and by the hand of his servants.
verses.arminianNotes: “These four were born to the giant in Gath; and they fell by the hand of David and by the hand of his servants.” Arminian readers see shared victory between the king and those who served with him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the summary crediting David and his servants together. Readers in this tradition note how the appendix leads from human victories to the song praising the LORD as deliverer.
